Provable Scaling Laws of Feature Emergence from Learning Dynamics of Grokking

Yuandong Tian
Meta Superintelligence Labs (FAIR) & Independent Researcher
yuandong.tian@gmail.com
Abstract

While the phenomenon of grokking, i.e., delayed generalization, has been studied extensively, it remains an open problem whether there is a mathematical framework that characterizes what kind of features will emerge, how and in which conditions it happens, and is still closely connected with the gradient dynamics of the training, for complex structured inputs. We propose a novel framework, named Li2, that captures three key stages for the grokking behavior of 2-layer nonlinear networks: (I) Lazy learning, (II) independent feature learning and (III) interactive feature learning. At the lazy learning stage, top layer overfits to random hidden representation and the model appears to memorize, and at the same time, the backpropagated gradient GFG_{F} from the top layer carries information about the target label, with a specific structure that enables each hidden node to learn their representation independently. Moreover, the independent dynamics follows exactly the gradient ascent of an energy function ℰ\mathcal{E}, and its local maxima are precisely the emerging features. We study whether these local-optima induced features are generalizable, their representation power, and how they change on sample size, in group arithmetic tasks. When hidden nodes start to interact in the later stage of learning, we provably show how GFG_{F} changes to focus on missing features that need to be learned. Our study sheds lights on roles played by key hyperparameters such as weight decay, learning rate and sample sizes in grokking, leads to provable scaling laws of feature emergence, memorization and generalization, and reveals the underlying cause why recent optimizers such as Muon can be effective, from the first principles of gradient dynamics. Our analysis can be extended to multi-layer architectures. The code is available111https://github.com/yuandong-tian/understanding/tree/main/ssl/real-dataset/cogo.

1 Introduction

While modern deep models such as Transformers have achieved impressive empirical performance, it remains a mystery how such models acquire the knowledge during the training process. There have been ongoing arguments on whether the models can truly generalize beyond what it is trained on, or just memorize the dataset and performs poorly in out-of-distribution (OOD) data (Wang et al., 2024b; Chu et al., 2025; Mirzadeh et al., 2024).

Modeling the memorization and generalization behaviors have been a goal of many works. One such behavior, know as grokking (Power et al., 2022; Doshi et al., 2024; Nanda et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024a; Varma et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Thilak et al., 2022), shows that the model initially overfits to the training set, and then suddenly generalizes to unseen test samples after continuous training. Many explanation exists, e.g., effective theory (Liu et al., 2022; Clauw et al., 2024), efficiency of memorization and generalization circuits (Varma et al., 2023), Bayesian interpretation with weight decay as prior (Millidge, 2022), etc. Most works focus on a direct explanation of its empirical behaviors, or leveraging property of very wide networks (Barak et al., 2022; Mohamadi et al., 2024; Rubin et al., 2024), but few explores the details of the grokking learning procedure by studying the gradient dynamics on the weights.

In this work, we propose a mathematical framework Li2 that divides the grokking dynamics for 2-layer nonlinear networks into three major stages (Fig. 1). Stage I: Lazy Learning: when training begins, the top (output) layer learns first with random features from the hidden layer, and at the same time, the backpropagated gradient GFG_{F} to the hidden layer starts to carry useful signal about the target label (Proposition 1). Stage II: Independent feature learning: GFG_{F} drives the learning of hidden representations. In this stage, the backpropagated gradient of jj-th neuron (node) only depends on its own activation, triggering independent feature learning for each node. Stage III: Interactive feature learning: When weights in the hidden layer get updated and are no longer independent, interactions across nodes adjust the learned feature to minimize the loss.

Each stage is studied in details. In Stage I, we show that the signal carried by the backpropagated gradient GFG_{F} either appears at the initial stage (Proposition 1) which depends on the top layer initialization, or the final stage (Lemma 1) which depends on the weight decay η\eta. In Stage II, we find that the dynamics that governs independent feature learning exactly follows the gradient ascent of an energy function ℰ\mathcal{E} (Thm. 1), which corresponds to nonlinear canonical-correlation analysis (CCA) between the input XX and target YY. In group arithmetic tasks, we completely characterize the local maxima structure of ℰ\mathcal{E} (Thm. 2), each representing one learned feature. We further show that the amount of training samples determine whether these features/local optima remain stable (Thm. 4), whether they are generalizable or not, and thus determine the scaling laws of generalization and memorization. In Stage III, we provably show that there is a push for diversity between hidden nodes with similar activations (Thm. 6), when a subset of features are learned, backpropagated gradient GFG_{F} changes to push the model to focus on missing features to minimize the loss (Thm. 7), and optimizers like Muon (Jordan et al., 2024) further improves the diversity (Thm. 8). Experiments on graph arithmetic tasks support our claims, e.g., the proved scaling laws about the generalization/memorization boundary (Thm. 4) fits well with the experiments (Fig. 5).

Comparison with existing grokking frameworks. Our framework provides a theoretical foundation from first principles (i.e., gradient dynamics) that explains the empirical hypothesis Varma et al. (2023) that “generalization circuits 𝒞g​e​n\mathcal{C}_{gen} is more efficient but learn slower than memorization circuits 𝒞m​e​m\mathcal{C}_{mem}”. Specifically, we show that the data distribution determines the optimization landscape, which in turn governs which local optima the weights converge into, which lead to the behavior of memorization or generalization. We also show that the initial memorization, or lazy learning (Stage I), has to happen before feature learning (Stage II-III), since the former provides meaningful backpropagated gradient GFG_{F} for the latter to start developing. In comparison, (Nanda et al., 2023) also provides a three stage framework of grokking, but mostly from empirical observations. Using our framework, we provide a systematic framework to explain when and why the grokking happens that are consistent with many empirical observations (Sec. 7).

Our study goes beyond Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) (Du et al., 2018; Jacot et al., 2018) and mean field regime (Rubin et al., 2024), in which the hidden weights do not update substantially from initializations. Our framework demonstrates concretely how features emerge from gradient dynamics and multiple key factors that affect the procedure.

Summary. Our framework Li2 splits the network training process into three stages (Lazy, independent, interactive), and provides insights into grokking dynamics and feature learning.

  • •

    Explanation of Grokking behavior. At the beginning of grokking, the lazy learning corresponds to memorization, in which the top layer finds a (temporary) solution to explain the target with the random features. Only after that, the backpropagated gradient GFG_{F} becomes meaningful, and causes the hidden layer to learn generalizable, emerging features. Grokking is accelerated with regularization.

  • •

    Emerging features are the local maxima of an energy function ℰ\mathcal{E} that governs the independent stage. These features are more efficient in label prediction than simple memorization.

  • •

    Data governs the landscape of ℰ\mathcal{E}. Sufficient training data maintain the shape of those generalizable local maxima, while insufficient data lead to non-generalizable local maxima.

  • •

    Scaling Laws of Feature Emergence, Generalization and Memorization can be derived by inspecting how the landscape changes with the data distribution.

2 Problem formulation

We consider a 2-layer network Y^=σ​(X​W)​V\hat{Y}=\sigma(XW)V and ℓ2\ell_{2} loss function on nn samples:

minV,W⁡12​‖P1⟂​(Y−Y^)‖F2=minV,W⁡12​‖P1⟂​(Y−σ​(X​W)​V)‖F2\min_{V,W}\frac{1}{2}\|P^{\perp}_{1}(Y-\hat{Y})\|_{F}^{2}=\min_{V,W}\frac{1}{2}\|P^{\perp}_{1}(Y-\sigma(XW)V)\|_{F}^{2} (1)

where P1⟂:=I−𝟏𝟏⊤/nP^{\perp}_{1}:=I-\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}/n is the zero-mean projection matrix along the sample dimension, Y∈ℝn×MY\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times M} is a label matrix (each row is a one-hot vector), X=[𝐱1,𝐱2,…,𝐱n]⊤∈ℝn×dX=[\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{2},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{n}]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} is the data matrix, V∈ℝK×MV\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times M} and W∈ℝd×KW\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times K} are the weight matrices of the last layer and hidden layer, respectively. σ\sigma is the nonlinear activation function.

In the following, we show that grokking is a consequence of “leaked” backpropagated gradient GFG_{F}.

3 Stage I: Lazy Learning (Overfitting)

Let F=σ​(X​W)F=\sigma(XW) be the activation of the hidden layer and F~=P1⟂​F\tilde{F}=P^{\perp}_{1}F be the zero-mean version of it. Similarly define Y~=P1⟂​Y\tilde{Y}=P^{\perp}_{1}Y. We first write down the backpropagated gradient GFG_{F} sent to the hidden layer:

GF=−∂J∂F=P1⟂​(Y−F​V)​V⊤G_{F}=-\frac{\partial J}{\partial F}=P^{\perp}_{1}(Y-FV)V^{\top} (2)

3.1 Analysis of the backpropagated gradient GFG_{F}

At the beginning of the training, both WW and VV are initialized with independent zero-mean random variables. Therefore, the backpropagated gradient GFG_{F} is pure random noise. Over time, the hidden activation FF is mostly unchanged, and only the output layer VV learns. In this case, FF can be treated as fixed during this stage of learning, and we can prove the following properties of GFG_{F} (Sec. C):

Proposition 1.

If F~\tilde{F} is fixed and is full column rank, entries of V​(0)V(0) is initialized from normal distribution N​(0,α2)N(0,\alpha^{2}) with 0<α≪10<\alpha\ll 1, then ‖GF​(0)‖F=O​(ϵ​K​M)\|G_{F}(0)\|_{F}=O(\epsilon\sqrt{KM}) and the backpropagated gradient GFG_{F} is dominated by the term Y~​Y~⊤​F\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}F at initial time stamps:

GF​(t)=t​Y~​Y~⊤​F~+O​(α)+O​(α​t)+O​(t2)G_{F}(t)=t{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}\tilde{F}}+O(\alpha)+O(\alpha t)+O(t^{2}) (3)

and converges exponentially to the following fixed point when V=Vridge=(F~⊤​F~+η​I)−1​F~⊤​Y~V=V_{\textrm{ridge}}=(\tilde{F}^{\top}\tilde{F}+\eta I)^{-1}\tilde{F}^{\top}\tilde{Y}:

GF​(+∞)=η​(F~​F~⊤+η​I)−1​Y~​Y~⊤​F~​(F~⊤​F~+η​I)−1G_{F}(+\infty)=\eta(\tilde{F}\tilde{F}^{\top}+\eta I)^{-1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}\tilde{F}}(\tilde{F}^{\top}\tilde{F}+\eta I)^{-1} (4)

GFG_{F} at initial phase. The proposition suggests that for small top layer initialization (measured by α\alpha), ‖GF‖\|G_{F}\| will first increase from O​(α)O(\alpha) to O​(1)O(1) and then converge exponentially to O​(η)O(\eta). Fig. 3 shows that this is indeed the case for ‖GF‖\|G_{F}\|, regardless whether grokking happens or not.

GFG_{F} at later phase. The structure of GF​(+∞)G_{F}(+\infty) is revealed by the following lemma:

Lemma 1 (Structure of backpropagated gradient GFG_{F}).

Assume that (1) entries of WW follow standard normal distribution N​(0,1)N(0,1), (2) ‖𝐱i‖2=const\|\mathbf{x}_{i}\|_{2}=\text{const}, (3) ‖𝐱i⊤​𝐱i′−ρ‖2≤ϵ\|\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{x}_{i^{\prime}}-\rho\|_{2}\leq\epsilon for all i≠i′i\neq i^{\prime} and (4) large width KK, then both F~⊤​F~\tilde{F}^{\top}\tilde{F} and F~​F~⊤\tilde{F}\tilde{F}^{\top} becomes a multiple of identity and Eqn. 4 becomes:

GF​(+∞)=η(K​c1+η)​(n​c2+η)​Y~​Y~⊤​F~+O​(K−1​ϵ)G_{F}(+\infty)=\frac{\eta}{(Kc_{1}+\eta)(nc_{2}+\eta)}\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}\tilde{F}+O(K^{-1}\epsilon) (5)

where c1,c2>0c_{1},c_{2}>0 are constants related to nonlinearity. When η\eta is small, we have GF∝η​Y~​Y~⊤​F~G_{F}\propto\eta\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}\tilde{F}. Note that the input features and/or weights can be scaled and what changes is c1c_{1} and c2c_{2}.

Interestingly, in both cases, we see that GFG_{F} contains a key term Y~​Y~⊤​F~{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}\tilde{F}}. As we will see, it plays a critical role in feature learning. From Eqn. 5, it is clear that if K→+∞K\rightarrow+\infty, then GF​(+∞)→0G_{F}(+\infty)\rightarrow 0 and there is no feature learning (i.e., NTK regime). Here we study the case when KK is large (so that Eqn. 5 is valid) but not too large so that feature learning happens.

3.2 Zero-init Accelerates the Feature Learning Process

Given the analysis in Sec. 3 of Stage I, it becomes tempting to think that if we initialize the top-layer weight VV to zero, then at the initial stage the backpropagated gradient GF​(t)G_{F}(t) carries only the signal term Y~​Y~⊤​F\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}F according to Eqn. 3, and the feature learning process should be accelerated. We named this new approach as zero-init.

Experiments show that this is indeed the case. Fig. 14, 15 and 16 show that for M=41,89,127M=41,89,127, zero-init accelerates the feature learning process compared to normal initialization.

In multi-layer setting, the boost brought up by zero-init is larger (Fig. 17), in particular when data are scarce and the feature learning process becomes slow. The gap can be as large as 10×10\times (e.g., 100 epochs versus 1000 epochs) when training on MSE loss.

All the experiments are in Appendix D.2.

4 Stage II: Independent feature learning

4.1 The energy function ℰ\mathcal{E}

Now let us explore the feature learning process with the help of GFG_{F}. Let W=[𝐰1,𝐰2,…,𝐰K]W=[\mathbf{w}_{1},\mathbf{w}_{2},\ldots,\mathbf{w}_{K}] where 𝐰j∈ℝd\mathbf{w}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is the weight vector of jj-th node, and F=[𝐟1,𝐟2,…,𝐟K]F=[\mathbf{f}_{1},\mathbf{f}_{2},\ldots,\mathbf{f}_{K}] where 𝐟j=σ​(X​𝐰j)∈ℝn\mathbf{f}_{j}=\sigma(X\mathbf{w}_{j})\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is the activation of jj-th node. For GF∝Y~​Y~⊤​F~G_{F}\propto\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}\tilde{F}, as the structure shown in both initial stage (Eqn. 3) and later stage (Eqn. 5), the jj-th column 𝐠j\mathbf{g}_{j} of GFG_{F} is only dependent on jj-th node 𝐰j\mathbf{w}_{j}, and thus we can decouple the dynamics into KK independent ones, each corresponding to a single node:

𝐰˙j=X⊤​Dj​𝐠j,𝐠j∝Y~​Y~⊤​σ​(X​𝐰j)\dot{\mathbf{w}}_{j}=X^{\top}D_{j}\mathbf{g}_{j},\quad\mathbf{g}_{j}\propto\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}\sigma(X\mathbf{w}_{j}) (6)

where Dj=diag​(σ′​(X​𝐰j))D_{j}=\text{diag}(\sigma^{\prime}(X\mathbf{w}_{j})) is the diagonal gating matrix of jj-th node. Note that Y~⊤​F=Y~⊤​F~\tilde{Y}^{\top}F=\tilde{Y}^{\top}\tilde{F} since P1⟂P^{\perp}_{1} is idempotent. A critical observation here is that Eqn. 6 actually corresponds to the gradient ascent dynamics of the energy function ℰ\mathcal{E}.

Theorem 1 (The energy function ℰ\mathcal{E} for independent feature learning).

The dynamics (Eqn. 6) of independent feature learning is exactly the gradient ascent dynamics of the energy function ℰ\mathcal{E} w.r.t. 𝐰j\mathbf{w}_{j}, a nonlinear canonical-correlation analysis (CCA) between the input XX and target Y~\tilde{Y}:

ℰ​(𝐰j)=12​‖Y~⊤​σ​(X​𝐰j)‖22\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{w}_{j})=\frac{1}{2}\|\tilde{Y}^{\top}\sigma(X\mathbf{w}_{j})\|^{2}_{2} (7)

Therefore, the feature learned for each node jj is the one that maximizes the energy function ℰ​(𝐰j)\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{w}_{j}). Since Eqn. 6 can be unbounded, in the following, we put an additional constraint that ‖𝐰j‖2=1\|\mathbf{w}_{j}\|_{2}=1 due to weight decay regularization. Note that (Tian, 2023) also arrives at an energy function when studying feature learning in the context of contrastive loss, the resulting function is abstract and difficult to interpret its structure of its local maxima. Here the structure is much clearer, which we will explore below.

4.2 Group Arithmetic Tasks

To demonstrate a concrete example in solving the energy function ℰ\mathcal{E}, we consider group arithmetic tasks, i.e., for group HH, the task is to predict h=h1​h2h=h_{1}h_{2} given h1,h2∈Hh_{1},h_{2}\in H. One example is the modular addition task h1​h2=h1+h2modMh_{1}h_{2}=h_{1}+h_{2}\mod M, which has been extensively studied in grokking (Power et al., 2022; Gromov, 2023; Huang et al., 2024; Tian, 2025).

Definition of group. Here h1​h2h_{1}h_{2} is the group operation of two elements h1h_{1} and h2h_{2} in the group HH. The group operation satisfies a few properties: (1) the group operation is associative, i.e., (h1​h2)​h3=h1​(h2​h3)(h_{1}h_{2})h_{3}=h_{1}(h_{2}h_{3}) for all h1,h2,h3∈Hh_{1},h_{2},h_{3}\in H, (2) there exists an identity element ee such that h​e=e​h=hhe=eh=h for all h∈Hh\in H, (3) for each h∈Hh\in H, there exists an inverse h−1h^{-1} such that h​h−1=h−1​h=ehh^{-1}=h^{-1}h=e. Note that the group operation is not commutative in general, i.e., h1​h2≠h2​h1h_{1}h_{2}\neq h_{2}h_{1} for some h1,h2∈Hh_{1},h_{2}\in H. If the operation is commutative, then we call the group Abelian. Modular addition is an example of Abelian group.

The task. We represent the group elements by one-hot vectors: each data sample 𝐱i∈ℝ2​M\mathbf{x}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{2M} is a concatenation of two MM-dimensional one-hot vectors (𝐞h1​[i],𝐞h2​[i])(\mathbf{e}_{h_{1}[i]},\mathbf{e}_{h_{2}[i]}) where h1​[i]h_{1}[i] and h2​[i]h_{2}[i] are the indices of the two one-hot vectors. The output is also a one-hot vector 𝐲i=𝐞h1​[i]​h2​[i]\mathbf{y}_{i}=\mathbf{e}_{h_{1}[i]h_{2}[i]}, where 1≤i≤n=M21\leq i\leq n=M^{2}. Here the class number M=|H|M=|H| is the size of the group.

A crash course of group representation theory. A mapping ρ​(h):H↦ℂd×d\rho(h):H\mapsto\mathbb{C}^{d\times d} is called a group representation if the group operation is compatible with matrix multiplication: ρ​(h1)​ρ​(h2)=ρ​(h1​h2)\rho(h_{1})\rho(h_{2})=\rho(h_{1}h_{2}) for any h1,h2∈Hh_{1},h_{2}\in H. Let Rh∈ℝM×MR_{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times M} be the regular representation of group element hh so that 𝐞h1​h2=Rh1​𝐞h2\mathbf{e}_{h_{1}h_{2}}=R_{h_{1}}\mathbf{e}_{h_{2}} for all h1,h2∈Hh_{1},h_{2}\in H, and P∈ℝM×MP\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times M} be the group inverse operator so that P​𝐞h=𝐞h−1P\mathbf{e}_{h}=\mathbf{e}_{h^{-1}}. Note that P2=IP^{2}=I and P⊤=P−1=PP^{\top}=P^{-1}=P.

A tale of two kind of “representations”. We often refer the activation vectors in neural network as “neural representations”, which means that we use high-dimensional vectors to represent certain semantic concepts (e.g., word2vec (Mikolov et al., 2013)). For groups, the group element corresponds to “transformation” / “action” that acts on one object and turn it to another (i.e., rotation of a vector). Therefore, group representations often take the form of matrices (e.g., permutation / rotation matrix).

The decomposition of group representation. The representation theory of finite group (Fulton & Harris, 2013; Steinberg, 2009) says that the regular representation RhR_{h} admits a decomposition into complex irreducible representations (or irreps):

Rh=Q​(⨁k=0κ​(H)⨁r=1mkCk​(h))​Q∗R_{h}=Q\left(\bigoplus_{k=0}^{\kappa(H)}\bigoplus_{r=1}^{m_{k}}C_{k}(h)\right)Q^{*} (8)

where κ​(H)\kappa(H) is the number of nontrivial irreps (i.e., not all hh map to identity), Ck​(h)∈ℂdk×dkC_{k}(h)\in\mathbb{C}^{d_{k}\times d_{k}} is the kk-th irrep block of RhR_{h}, QQ is the unitary matrix (and Q∗Q^{*} is its conjugate transpose) and mkm_{k} is the multiplicity of the kk-th irrep. This means that in the decomposition of RhR_{h}, there are mkm_{k} copies of dkd_{k}-dimensional irrep, and these copies are isomorphic to each other. So the kk-th irrep subspace ℋk\mathcal{H}_{k} has dimension mk​dkm_{k}d_{k}.

For regular representation {Rh}\{R_{h}\}, one can prove that mk=dkm_{k}=d_{k} for all kk and thus |H|=M=∑kdk2|H|=M=\sum_{k}d^{2}_{k}. For Abelian group, all complex irreps are 1d (i.e., Fourier bases). One may also choose to do the decomposition in real domain. In this case, a pair of 1d complex irreps will become a 2d real irrep. For example, ei​θe^{\mathrm{i}\theta} and e−i​θe^{-\mathrm{i}\theta} becomes a 2d matrix [cos⁡(θ),−sin⁡(θ);sin⁡(θ),cos⁡(θ)][\cos(\theta),-\sin(\theta);\sin(\theta),\cos(\theta)].

4.3 Local maxima of the energy function

Now we study the local maxima of ℰ\mathcal{E}. With the decomposition, we can completely characterize the local maxima of the energy ℰ\mathcal{E} with group inputs, even that ℰ​(𝐰)\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{w}) is nonconvex.

Theorem 2 (Local maxima of ℰ\mathcal{E} for group input).

For group arithmetics tasks with σ​(x)=x2\sigma(x)=x^{2}, ℰ\mathcal{E} has multiple local maxima 𝐰∗=[𝐮;±P​𝐮]\mathbf{w}^{\ast}=[\mathbf{u};\pm P\mathbf{u}]. Either it is in a real irrep of dimension dkd_{k} (with ℰ∗=M/8​dk\mathcal{E}^{\ast}=M/8d_{k} and 𝐮∈ℋk\mathbf{u}\in\mathcal{H}_{k}), or in a pair of complex irrep of dimension dkd_{k} (with ℰ∗=M/16​dk\mathcal{E}^{\ast}=M/16d_{k} and 𝐮∈ℋk⊕ℋk¯\mathbf{u}\in\mathcal{H}_{k}\oplus\mathcal{H}_{\bar{k}}). These local maxima are not connected. No other local maxima exist.

Note that our proof can be extended to more general nonlinearity σ​(x)=a​x+b​x2\sigma(x)=ax+bx^{2} with b>0b>0 since linear part will be cancelled out due to zero-mean operators. We can show that local maxima of ℰ\mathcal{E} are flat, allowing moving around without changing ℰ\mathcal{E}:

Corollary 1 (Flatness of local maxima of ℰ\mathcal{E} for group input).

Local maxima of ℰ\mathcal{E} for group arithmetics tasks with |H|=M>2|H|=M>2 are flat, i.e., at least one eigenvalue of its Hessian is zero.

We can apply the above theorem to the popular modular addition task which is an Abelian group. The resulting representation is Fourier bases.

Corollary 2 (Modular addition).

For modular addition with odd MM, all local maxima are single frequency 𝐮k=ak​[cos⁡(k​m​ω)]m=0M−1+bk​[sin⁡(k​m​ω)]m=0M−1\mathbf{u}_{k}=a_{k}[\cos(km\omega)]_{m=0}^{M-1}+b_{k}[\sin(km\omega)]_{m=0}^{M-1} where ω:=2​π/M\omega:=2\pi/M with ℰ∗=M/16\mathcal{E}^{\ast}=M/16. For even MM, 𝐮M/2∝[(−1)m]m=0M−1\mathbf{u}_{M/2}\propto[(-1)^{m}]_{m=0}^{M-1} has ℰ∗=M/8\mathcal{E}^{\ast}=M/8. Different local maxima are disconnected.

Role played by the nonlinearity. Note that if σ​(x)\sigma(x) is linear, then there is no local maxima, but only a global one, which is the maximal eigenvector of X⊤​Y~​Y~⊤​XX^{\top}\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}X. This corresponds to Linear Discriminative Analysis (LDA) (Balakrishnama & Ganapathiraju, 1998) that finds directions that maximally separate the class-mean vectors. For group arithmetics tasks, for each target h=h1​h2h=h_{1}h_{2}, each group element (h1h_{1} and h2h_{2}) appears once and only once, the class-mean vectors are identical and thus LDA fails to identify any meaningful directions. With nonlinearity, the learned 𝐰\mathbf{w} has clear meanings.

Meaning of the learned features. First, the learned representation can offer a more efficient reconstruction of the target (see Thm. 3) than simple memorization of all M2M^{2} pairs. Second, learned representations naturally contain useful invariance. For example, some irreps of the cyclic group of ℤ15\mathbb{Z}_{15} behave like its subgroup ℤ3\mathbb{Z}_{3} and ℤ5\mathbb{Z}_{5}, by mapping its element hh to div​(h,3)\mathrm{div}(h,3) and div​(h,5)\mathrm{div}(h,5). If we regard hh to be controlled by two hidden factors, then these features lead to focusing on one factor and invariant to others. More importantly, they emerge automatically without explicit supervision.

4.4 Representation power of learned features

With Thm. 2, we know that each node of the hidden layers will learn various representations. The question is whether they are sufficient to reconstruct the target Y~\tilde{Y} and how efficient they are.

Theorem 3 (Target Reconstruction).

Assume (1) ℰ\mathcal{E} is optimized in complex domain ℂ\mathbb{C}, (2) for each irrep kk, there are mk2​dk2m^{2}_{k}d^{2}_{k} pairs of learned weights 𝐰=[𝐮;±P​𝐮]\mathbf{w}=[\mathbf{u};\pm P\mathbf{u}] whose associated rank-1 matrices {𝐮𝐮∗}\{\mathbf{u}\mathbf{u}^{*}\} form a complete bases for ℋk\mathcal{H}_{k} and (3) the top layer VV also learns with η=0\eta=0, then Y^=Y~\hat{Y}=\tilde{Y}.

From the theorem, we know that K=2​∑k≠0mk2​dk2≤2​[(M−κ​(H))2+κ​(H)−1]K=2\sum_{k\neq 0}m^{2}_{k}d^{2}_{k}\leq 2\left[(M-\kappa(H))^{2}+\kappa(H)-1\right] suffice. In particular, for Abelian group, κ​(H)=M−1\kappa(H)=M-1 and K=2​M−2K=2M-2. This is much more efficient than a pure memorization solution that would require M2M^{2} nodes, i.e., each node memorizes a single pair (h1,h2)∈H×H(h_{1},h_{2})\in H\times H.

Assumptions of the theorem. Training the model in an end-to-end manner automatically satisfies the assumption (3). If we initialize the weights randomly, then with high probability, the resulting 𝐮\mathbf{u} are not collinear and the assumption (2) can be satisfied. For assumption (1), interestingly, no such theorem can be stated in the real domain ℝ\mathbb{R}, because in ℝ\mathbb{R}, the subspace of orthogonal matrices, which group representations belong to, is not covered by the subspace of symmetric matrices spanned by {𝐮𝐮⊤}\{\mathbf{u}\mathbf{u}^{\top}\}. In contrast, in the complex domain ℂ\mathbb{C}, the subspace of unitary matrices can be represented by Hermitian matrices. Does that mean that the real representation is not that useful? Not really. If we change 𝐰=[𝐮;±P​𝐮]\mathbf{w}=[\mathbf{u};\pm P\mathbf{u}] slightly to 𝐰=[𝐮;±P​𝐮′]\mathbf{w}=[\mathbf{u};\pm P\mathbf{u}^{\prime}] in which 𝐮′\mathbf{u}^{\prime} is a small perturbation of 𝐮\mathbf{u}, then Thm. 3 holds for real solutions. This happens in the stage III when end-to-end backpropagation refines the representation. Fig. 11 shows that using complex weights still works and may grok faster.

4.5 The Scaling Laws of the boundary of memorization and generalization

While Thm. 2 shows the nice structure of local maxima (and features learned), it requires training on all n=M2n=M^{2} pairs of group elements. One may ask whether these representations can still be learned if training on a subset. The answer is yes, by checking the stability of the local maximum.

Theorem 4 (Amount of samples to maintain local optima).

If we select n≳dk2​M​log⁡(M/δ)n\gtrsim d_{k}^{2}M\log(M/\delta) data sample from H×HH\times H uniformly at random, then with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, the empirical energy function ℰ^\hat{\mathcal{E}} keeps local maxima for dkd_{k}-dimensional irreps (Thm. 2).

The theorem above says that we do not need all M2M^{2} samples, but only O​(M​log⁡M)O(M\log M) samples suffice to learn these features, which will generalize to unseen data according to Thm. 3. Fig. 5 demonstrates that the empirical results closely match the theoretical prediction, and there is a clear phase transition around the boundary (test accuracy 0→10\rightarrow 1), where the training data ratio p:=n/M2=O​(M−1​log⁡M)p:=n/M^{2}=O(M^{-1}\log M).

Memorization. On the other hand, we can also construct cases when memorization is the only local maximum of ℰ\mathcal{E}. This happens when we only collect samples for one target hh but missing others, and diversity is in question.

Theorem 5 (Memorization solution).

Let ϕ​(x):=σ′​(x)/x\phi(x):=\sigma^{\prime}(x)/x and assume σ′​(x)>0\sigma^{\prime}(x)>0 for x>0x>0. For group arithmetic tasks, suppose we only collect sample (g,g−1​h)(g,g^{-1}h) for one target hh with probability pgp_{g}. Then the global optimal of ℰ\mathcal{E} is a memorization solution, either (1) a focused memorization 𝐰=12​(𝐞g∗,𝐞g∗−1​h)\mathbf{w}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\mathbf{e}_{g^{*}},\mathbf{e}_{g^{*-1}h}) for g∗=arg⁡max⁡pgg^{*}=\arg\max p_{g} if ϕ\phi is nondecreasing, or (2) a spreading memorization with 𝐰=12​∑gsg​[𝐞g,𝐞g−1​h]\mathbf{w}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{g}s_{g}[\mathbf{e}_{g},\mathbf{e}_{g^{-1}h}], if ϕ\phi is strictly decreasing. Here sg=ϕ−1​(2​λ/pg)s_{g}=\phi^{-1}(2\lambda/p_{g}) and λ\lambda is determined by ∑gsg2=2\sum_{g}s_{g}^{2}=2. No other local optima exist.

We can verify that power activations (e.g., σ​(x)=x2\sigma(x)=x^{2}) lead to focused memorization, while more practical ones (e.g., ReLU, SiLU, Tanh and Sigmoid) lead to spreading memorization. We leave it for future work whether this property leads to better results in large scale settings.

Boundary of generalization and memorization (semi-grokking (Varma et al., 2023)). In between the two extreme cases, local maxima of both memorization and generalization may co-exist. In this case, small learning rate keeps the optimization within the attractive basin and converges to gsol, while large learning rate leads to ngsol which has better energy ℰ\mathcal{E} (Fig. 7).

Our analysis fits well with the observed empirical behaviors that there exists a critical data size (Varma et al., 2023) or more precisely a critical data ratio (Wang et al., 2024a; Abramov et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2022), above which the grokking suddenly leads to generalization. Our framework Li2 gives a theory-backed explanation: different data distribution leads to different landscapes, which gives either generalization or memorization local maxima that the weights will fall into. It also explains the ungrokking phenomenon: a grokked model can move back to memorization when continues to train on a smaller dataset (Varma et al., 2023), and is consistent with (Nguyen & Reddy, 2025) that shows that task diversity is important for generalization. The empirical hypothesis (e.g., “memorization/generalization circuits”) now becomes a natural consequence of changed landscape after training.

5 Stage III: Interactive feature learning

The starting point of Stage II is to simplify the exact backpropagated gradient GF=Pη​Y~​Y~⊤​F~​BG_{F}=P_{\eta}\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}\tilde{F}B (Eqn. 4) with B:=(F~⊤​F~+η​I)−1B:=(\tilde{F}^{\top}\tilde{F}+\eta I)^{-1} to GF∝η​Y~​Y~⊤​FG_{F}\propto\eta\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}F, by two approximations: (1) B∝IB\propto I, and (2) Pη∝η​IP_{\eta}\propto\eta I. The two approximations are valid due to Thm. 1 when the hidden weights WW is randomly initialized. When training continues, WW evolves from random initialization and the conditions may not hold anymore. In this section we put them back and study their behaviors.

5.1 Repulsion of similar features

We first study the effect of BB, which leads to interplay of hidden nodes. Over the training, the activations of two nodes can be highly correlated and the following theorem shows that similar features leads to repulsion.

Theorem 6 (Repulsion of similar features).

The jj-th column of F~​B\tilde{F}B is given by:

[F~​B]j=bj​j​𝐟~j+∑l=1Kbj​l​𝐟~l[\tilde{F}B]_{j}=b_{jj}\tilde{\mathbf{f}}_{j}+\sum_{l=1}^{K}b_{jl}\tilde{\mathbf{f}}_{l} (9)

where sign​(bj​l)=−sign​(𝐟~j⊤​Pη,−j​l​𝐟~l)\mathrm{sign}(b_{jl})=-\mathrm{sign}(\tilde{\mathbf{f}}_{j}^{\top}P_{\eta,-jl}\tilde{\mathbf{f}}_{l}). Here Pη,−j​l:=I−F~−j​l​(F~−j​l⊤​F~−j​l+η​I)−1​F~−j​l⊤P_{\eta,-jl}:=I-\tilde{F}_{-jl}(\tilde{F}_{-jl}^{\top}\tilde{F}_{-jl}+\eta I)^{-1}\tilde{F}_{-jl}^{\top} is a projection matrix constructed from F~−j​l\tilde{F}_{-jl}, which is F~\tilde{F} excluding the ll-th and jj-th columns.

Remark. Intuitively, if 𝐟~j\tilde{\mathbf{f}}_{j} and 𝐟~l\tilde{\mathbf{f}}_{l} are similar, then bj​lb_{jl} will be negative and the resulting jj and ll columns of F~​B\tilde{F}B will be pushed away from each other and vise versa.

5.2 Top-down Modulation

Over the training process, it is possible that some local optima are learned first while others learned later. When the representations are learned partially, the backpropagation offers a mechanism to focus on missing pieces, by changing the landscape of the energy function ℰ\mathcal{E}.

Theorem 7 (Top-down Modulation).

For group arithmetic tasks with σ​(x)=x2\sigma(x)=x^{2}, if the hidden layer learns only a subset 𝒮\mathcal{S} of irreps, then the backpropagated gradient GF∝(Φ𝒮⊗𝟏M)​(Φ𝒮⊗𝟏M)∗​FG_{F}\propto(\Phi_{\mathcal{S}}\otimes\mathbf{1}_{M})(\Phi_{\mathcal{S}}\otimes\mathbf{1}_{M})^{\ast}F (see proof for the definition of Φ𝒮\Phi_{\mathcal{S}}), which yields a modified ℰ𝒮\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{S}} that only has local maxima on the missing irreps k∉𝒮k\notin\mathcal{S}.

5.3 Diversity enhancement with Muon

In addition to the mechanism above, certain optimizers (e.g., Muon optimizer (Jordan et al., 2024)) can also address such issue, by boosting the weight update direction that are underrepresented, enforcing diversity of nodes. While evidence (Tveit et al., 2025) and analysis exist (Shen et al., 2025) to show that Muon has advantages over other optimizers, to our best knowledge, we are the first to analyze it in the context of feature learning.

Recall that the Muon optimizer converts the gradient GW=UGW​D​VGW⊤G_{W}=U_{G_{W}}DV_{G_{W}}^{\top} (its SVD decomposition) to GW′=UGW​VGW⊤G^{\prime}_{W}=U_{G_{W}}V_{G_{W}}^{\top} and update the weight WW accordingly (i.e., W˙∝GW′\dot{W}\propto G^{\prime}_{W}). We first show that when Muon is applied to independent feature learning on each 𝐰j\mathbf{w}_{j} to make them coupled, it still gives the correct answers to the original optimization problems.

Lemma 2 (Muon optimizes the same as gradient flow).

Muon finds ascending direction to maximize the joint energy function ℰjoint​(W)=∑jℰ​(𝐰j)\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{joint}}(W)=\sum_{j}\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{w}_{j}) and has stationary points iff the original gradient GWG_{W} vanishes.

Now we show that Muon optimizer can rebalance the gradient updates.

Theorem 8 (Muon rebalances gradient updates).

Consider the following dynamics (Tian, 2023):

𝐰˙=A​(𝐰)​𝐰,‖𝐰‖2≤1\dot{\mathbf{w}}=A(\mathbf{w})\mathbf{w},\quad\quad\|\mathbf{w}\|_{2}\leq 1 (10)

where A​(𝐰):=∑lλl​(𝐰)​𝛇l​𝛇l⊤A(\mathbf{w}):=\sum_{l}\lambda_{l}(\mathbf{w})\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{l}\boldsymbol{\zeta}^{\top}_{l}. Assume that (1) {𝛇l}\{\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{l}\} form orthonormal bases, (2) for 𝐰=∑lαl​𝛇l\mathbf{w}=\sum_{l}\alpha_{l}\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{l}, we have λl​(𝐰)=μl​αl\lambda_{l}(\mathbf{w})=\mu_{l}\alpha_{l} with μl≤1\mu_{l}\leq 1, and (3) {αl}\{\alpha_{l}\} is initialized from inverse-exponential distribution with CDF​(x)=exp⁡(−x−a)\mathrm{CDF}(x)=\exp(-x^{-a}) with a>1a>1. Then

  • •

    Independent feature learning. Pr⁡[𝐰→𝜻l]=pl:=μla/∑lμla\Pr[\mathbf{w}\rightarrow\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{l}]=p_{l}:=\mu_{l}^{a}/\sum_{l}\mu_{l}^{a}. Then the expected #nodes to get all local maxima is T0≥max⁡(1/minl⁡pl,∑l=1L1/l)T_{0}\geq\max\left(1/\min_{l}p_{l},\sum_{l=1}^{L}1/l\right).

  • •

    Muon guiding. If we use Muon optimizer to optimize KK nodes sequentially, then the expected #nodes to get all local maxima is Ta=2−a​T0+(1−2−a)​LT_{a}=2^{-a}T_{0}+(1-2^{-a})L. For large aa, Ta∼LT_{a}\sim L.

The intuition here is that once some weight vectors have “occupied” a local maximum, say 𝜻m\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{m}, their gradients point to the same direction (before projecting onto the unit sphere ‖𝐰‖2=1\|\mathbf{w}\|_{2}=1), and the gradient correction of Muon will discount that component from gradients of currently optimized weight vectors, and keeping them away from 𝜻m\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{m}. In this way, Muon pressed novel gradient directions and thus encourages exploration. Fig. 8 shows that Muon is effective with limited number of hidden nodes KK.

Note that Eqn. 10 is closely related to ℰ\mathcal{E}, under the assumption of homogeneous/reversible activation, i.e., σ​(x)=C​σ′​(x)​x\sigma(x)=C\sigma^{\prime}(x)x with a constant CC (Zhao et al., 2024; Tian et al., 2020). In such setting, Eqn. 6 is related to the gradient dynamics with a PSD matrix A​(𝐰)=X⊤​D​(𝐰)​Y~​Y~⊤​D​(𝐰)​XA(\mathbf{w})=X^{\top}D(\mathbf{w})\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}D(\mathbf{w})X.

6 Extension to deeper architectures

The above analysis and the definition of the energy function ℰ\mathcal{E} can be extended to deeper architectures. Consider a multi-layer network with LL hidden layers, Fl=σ​(Fl−1​Wl)F_{l}=\sigma(F_{l-1}W_{l}) with F0=XF_{0}=X and Y^=FL​V\hat{Y}=F_{L}V. For notation brevity, let Gl:=GFlG_{l}:=G_{F_{l}}. Let’s see how the gradient backpropagated and how the learning fits to our framework (Fig. 1).

Stage I. Stage I does not change since FLF_{L} is still a random representation. Then when VV starts to learn and converges, the backpropagated gradient GLG_{L} now carries meaningful information: GL∝Y~​Y~⊤​FLG_{L}\propto\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}F_{L} (Eqn. 5), which initiates Stage II.

Stage II. We assume homogeneous activation σ​(x)=C​σ′​(x)​x\sigma(x)=C\sigma^{\prime}(x)x. For the next layer L−1L-1, we have:

GL−1=DL​GL​WL⊤=DL​(Y~​Y~⊤​FL)​WL⊤=(DL​Y~​Y~⊤​DL)​FL−1​(WL​WL⊤)G_{L-1}=D_{L}G_{L}W_{L}^{\top}=D_{L}(\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}F_{L})W_{L}^{\top}=(D_{L}\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}D_{L})F_{L-1}(W_{L}W_{L}^{\top}) (11)

since WLW_{L} is randomly initialized, we have WL​WL⊤≈IW_{L}W_{L}^{\top}\approx I and thus GL−1∝DL​Y~​Y~⊤​DL​FL−1G_{L-1}\propto D_{L}\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}D_{L}F_{L-1}.

Doing this iteratively gives Gl∝(D~l+1​Y~​Y~⊤​D~l+1)​FlG_{l}\propto\left(\tilde{D}_{l+1}\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}\tilde{D}_{l+1}\right)F_{l}, where D~l:=∏m=lLDm\tilde{D}_{l}:=\prod_{m=l}^{L}D_{m}. Note that these DD matrices are essentially reweighing/pruning samples randomly, since right now all {Wl}\{W_{l}\} are random except for VV. Now the lowest layer receives meaningful backpropagated gradient G1G_{1} that is related to the target label, and it also exposes to input XX. Therefore, the learning starts from there. Once layer ll learns decent representation, layer l+1l+1 receives meaningful input FlF_{l} and starts to learn, etc. When layer ll is learning, layer l′>ll^{\prime}>l do not learn since their input Fl′F_{l^{\prime}} remains random noise.

From this analysis, we can also see why residual connection helps. In this case, Gres,1=∑l=1LGlG_{\mathrm{res},1}=\sum_{l=1}^{L}G_{l}, in which GLG_{L} is definitely a much cleaner and stronger signal, compared to G1G_{1} which undergoes many random reweighing and pruning of samples.

Stage III. Once the activation FlF_{l} becomes meaningful, top-down modulation could happen (similar to Thm. 7) among nearby layers so that low-level features can be useful to support high-level representations. We leave the detailed analysis for future work.

7 When does grokking happen?

We first want to clarify that grokking (i.e., delayed generalization) is a phenomenon/observation that may suggest multiple underlying situations. When we observe “grokking happens”, it is often the case that the training gets stuck in lazy learning for a while before moving to feature learning. On the other hand, when we observe ”grokking does not happen”, then we may fall into one of the three very different situations: (1) training simply gets stuck in lazy training, (2) feature learning happens very early and the gap between training and test performance is always small, or (3) feature learning has converged to non-generalizable solutions due to e.g., insufficient or noisy data, and thus test performance is never improved. Note that (2) is a very good outcome while (1) and (3) are bad ones.

Therefore, it would be tricky to directly relate the hyperparameters with grokking behaviors. Instead, using Li2 framework, we focus on relating them with the backpropagated gradient GFG_{F} and the underlying feature learning process, which is more fundamental. Only when the GFG_{F} become large and sends a sufficient “amount” of the key term Y~​Y~⊤​F\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}F down to the hidden layers, grokking could happen. Here we categorize these factors into several categories.

Learning rate.  (Gromov, 2023) reports that grokking happens without regularization, but with a large initial learning rate (verified by the author). This corresponds to increasing the strength of GF​(t)∝t​Y~​Y~⊤​FG_{F}(t)\propto t\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}F at the initial phase of learning so that the hidden layers receives enough correct gradient signal to start the feature learning.

Stay longer before overfitting.  (Prieto et al., 2025) uses stable softmax (linear form) rather than regular softmax (exponential form) in computing probability. This prevents the model from overfitting to the label too quickly, and thus maintains a nonzero backpropagated gradient that can be useful for feature learning. (Kumar et al., 2024) also reports that grokking happens without regularization, using vanilla SGD optimizer. Our explanation is that it may take longer for SGD to converge to VridgeV_{\textrm{ridge}} than Adam, and during that period, the hidden layer has already accumulated a sufficient amount of correct gradient signal.

Weight initialization.  (Liu et al., 2023) reports that grokking happens with small initialization, regardless of the weight decay. This is straightforward from our framework, since GF​(t)=O​(α)+t​Y~​Y~⊤​F+O​(α​t)+O​(t2)G_{F}(t)=O(\alpha)+t\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}F+O(\alpha t)+O(t^{2}) and if the weight initialization α\alpha is small, then GF​(t)G_{F}(t) is dominated by clear signal term t​Y~​Y~⊤​F~t\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}\tilde{F}, which leads to fast feature learning. If α\alpha is large, then O​(α)O(\alpha) term is large and the initial phase of GFG_{F} contains too much noise, and we need to rely on the signal provided by the convergence phrase of GFG_{F} controlled by the weight decay η\eta. This is consistent with the finding by (Liu et al., 2023) that for large weight initialization, regularization is needed for grokking to happen, and small regularization leads to slow grokking transition.

Scaling factor β\beta of the output.  (Kumar et al., 2024; Chizat et al., 2019) reports that scaling the output by a factor β>1\beta>1 will make the grokking faster. From Li2 framework, this corresponds to optimizing Jβ​(V)=‖Y~−β​F~​V‖F2+η​‖V‖F2J_{\beta}(V)=\|\tilde{Y}-\beta\tilde{F}V\|^{2}_{F}+\eta\|V\|^{2}_{F}. Following a similar derivation as in Sec. C, in Sec. C.3 we can show that at the initial phase, the backpropagated gradient GF​(t)=O​(α)+t​[β​Y~​Y~⊤​F~+O​(β2​α)+O​(β3​α2)]+O​(t2)G_{F}(t)=O(\alpha)+t\left[\beta\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}\tilde{F}+O(\beta^{2}\alpha)+O(\beta^{3}\alpha^{2})\right]+O(t^{2}). So if β>1\beta>1 is large and the initialization α≪1\alpha\ll 1 then the signal term t​β​Y~​Y~⊤​F~t\beta\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}\tilde{F} becomes more dominant than the case of β=1\beta=1, and the grokking happens faster. However, if we have too large β\beta over α\alpha, then the term O​(β2​α)O(\beta^{2}\alpha) may cause trouble in feature learning and the final GF​(+∞)G_{F}(+\infty) becomes small (Eqn. 69). Equivalently, same theory applies if we downscale the target label (Kumar et al., 2024).

Weight decay η\eta. According to Eqn. 4, since GF​(+∞)∝η​Y~​Y~⊤​FG_{F}(+\infty)\propto\eta\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}F, it is clear that the weight decay η\eta becomes the learning rate of feature learning process. This coincides with findings in empirical works (Power et al., 2022; Clauw et al., 2024) that low regularization leads to slow grokking transition. This is also consistent with t∼1/ηt\sim 1/\eta laws to start grokking (Liu et al., 2023) or reach maximal test performance (Lewkowycz & Gur-Ari, 2020).

Data size nn. Our sample analysis (Theorem. 4) shows the local maxima can be kept with sufficient number of samples (n≳M​log⁡Mn\gtrsim M\log M). Intuitively, more samples lead to better shaped local maxima with less noise and thus the feature learning is faster, which is consistent with (Power et al., 2022; Nanda et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024a; Gromov, 2023; Abramov et al., 2025).

The number of hidden nodes KK. Our analysis requires that we need a decent number of hidden nodes KK to cover the diverse set of the local maxima of ℰ\mathcal{E}. On the other hand, Lemma 1 tells that very large KK may reduce |GF​(+∞)||G_{F}(+\infty)| and makes grokking slower. This is consistent with the finding by (Chizat et al., 2019) and NTK regime (Du et al., 2018; Jacot et al., 2018) that feature learning does not happen.

Early stopping. Model may overfit after generalization Montanari & Urbani (2025). Our framework shows that if data are scarce, generalization solutions have lower energy than memorization ones. If trained long enough, weights will move to solutions with larger ℰ\mathcal{E}.

8 Discussion

Relationship between grokking and regularization. A key insight of the Li2 framework is that a non-zero backpropagated gradient GFG_{F} initiates the feature learning process, setting the stage for optimizing the energy function ℰ\mathcal{E} that determines which features are learned and how. Intuitively, as long as the lazy learning phase produces a sufficiently large nonzero GFG_{F} correlated with the target label YY, feature learning will be triggered.

Several ways exist to ensure this nonzero gradient. Regularization mechanisms, such as weight decay, help guarantee the presence of a nonzero GFG_{F}, and conveniently allow us to demonstrate the feature learning process in a mathematically rigorous way. However, we want to emphasize that regularization is not the only option. For example, GFG_{F} might become large during lazy learning and later vanish due to perfect overfitting (see Eqn. 4). Notably, (Prieto et al., 2024) replaces the standard softmax (exponential term) with a stable softmax (linear term), which from the perspective of the Li2 framework, slows down overfitting to the labels. This maintains a nonzero backpropagated gradient, thereby preserving the potential for subsequent feature learning.

In summary, our framework shows that weight decay can be a sufficient condition for feature learning (and grokking), but not a necessary one.

Two different kinds of memorization. From the analysis, it is clear that memorization of grokking stems from overfitting on random features, which is different from landing on memorization solutions following the feature learning dynamics due to limited/noisy data (Thm. 5). From this view, grokking does not switch from memorization to generalization, but switch from overfitting to generalization.

Flat versus sharp optima. Common knowledge often regards flat optima as generalizable solutions, while sharp optima as memorization/overfitting. From the point of view of Li2, sharp optima happen when the model overfits on random features (Sec. 3), and thus small changes of the weights will change the loss a lot. On the other hand, we can prove that the local optima from ℰ\mathcal{E} are flat (Corollary 1), and thus small changes of the weights at certain directions do not change ℰ\mathcal{E}. If the model is over-parameterized, then multiple nodes may learn the same (or similar) set of features, which create freedom for the loss function to be flat. If we learn memorizing features due to limited/noisy data (Thm. 5), then more nodes need to be involved to “explain” the target well, and the overall weights will appear to be less flat.

Small versus large learning rates. According to our analysis, in Stage I, we need large learning rate to quickly learn ridge solution VV so that the backpropagated gradient GFG_{F} becomes meaningful to trigger Stage II. In Stage II, the best learning rate depends on the amount of data available. With a lot of data, we can afford larger learning rate to find the features quickly. With limited data, we may need smaller learning rate to stay in the basins of generalizable features (Fig. 7), which may be contradictory to common belief.

9 Related Works

Explanation of Grokking. Multiple explanations of grokking exist, e.g., competition of generalization and memorization circuits (Merrill et al., 2023), a shift from lazy to rich regimes Kumar et al. (2024), etc. Dynamics of grokking is analyzed in specific circumstance, e.g., for clustering data (Xu et al., 2023), linear network (Dominé et al., 2024), etc. In comparison, our work studies the full dynamics of feature emergence driven by backpropagation in group arithmetic tasks for deep nonlinear networks, and provide a systematic mathematical framework about what and how features emerge and a scaling law about when the transition between memorization and generalization happens.

Usage of group structure. Recent work leverages group theory to study the structure of final grokked solutions (Tian, 2025; Morwani et al., 2023; Shutman et al., 2025). None of them tackle the dynamics of grokking in the presence of the underlying structure of the data as we do.

Scaling laws of memorization and generalization. Previous works have identified scaling laws for memorization/generalization (Nguyen & Reddy, 2025; Wang et al., 2024a; Abramov et al., 2025; Doshi et al., 2023) without systematic theoretical explanation. Our work models such transitions as whether generalizable local optima remain stable under data sampling, and provide theoretical framework from first principles.

Feature learning. Previous works treats the NTK as a holistic object and study how it moves away from lazy regime, e.g., it becomes more correlated with task-relevant directions (Kumar et al., 2024; Ba et al., 2022; Damian et al., 2022), becomes adapted to the data (Rubin et al., 2025; Karp et al., 2021), etc. In contrast, our work focuses on explicit learning dynamics of individual features, their interactions, and the transition from memorization to generalization with more samples.

10 Conclusion, Limitations, and Future Work

We develop a principled mathematical framework Li2 for the grokking dynamics in 2-layer networks. Li2 identifies three stages, lazy learning, independent feature learning, and interactive feature learning, each marked by distinct structure of backpropagated gradient GFG_{F}. Weight decay enables hidden nodes to independently extract label-related features via a well-defined energy function ℰ\mathcal{E}, before cross interactions consolidate them. The analysis clarifies how hyperparameters like weight decay, learning rate, and sample size shape grokking, and offers first principles insight into why modern optimizers (e.g., Muon) are effective. We also extend our framework to deeper networks.

Limitations. While the derivation of energy ℰ\mathcal{E} is applicable to any input, analysis of its local maxima relies on restrictive assumption of group structure of the input. Also our analysis does not include the transition time between consecutive learning stages. We leave them for future work.

Disclosure of LLM usage

We have used SoTA LLMs extensively to brainstorm ideas to prove mathematical statements presented in the paper. Specifically, we setup research directions, provide problem setup and intuitions, proposes statements for LLM to analyze and prove, points out key issues in the generated proofs, adjust the statements accordingly and iterate. We also have done extensive experiments to verify the resulting statements. Many proofs proposed by LLMs are incorrect in subtle ways and requires substantial editing and correction. We have carefully revised all the proofs presented in the work, and take full accountability for their correctness.

Ethics Statement

This work is about investigating various theoretical and empirical properties of neural networks. We do not rely on any sensitive or proprietary data, nor do we use any existing open source models that may produce harmful contents.

Reproducibility Statement

All datasets used in this work can be generated synthetically. Models are pretrained from scratch with very small amount of compute. We will release code to support full Reproducibility.

Lemma 4 (Moment identity).

For X∼𝒩​(0,1)X\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1), 𝔼​[et​X]=exp⁡(t2/2)\mathbb{E}[e^{tX}]=\exp(t^{2}/2). Equivalently, 𝔼​[et​X−t2/2]=1\mathbb{E}[e^{tX-t^{2}/2}]=1.

𝔼​[et​X]=12​π​∫ℝet​x​e−x2/2​𝑑x=12​π​∫e−(x−t)2/2​et2/2​𝑑x=exp⁡(t22).\mathbb{E}[e^{tX}]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{tx}e^{-x^{2}/2}\,dx=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int e^{-(x-t)^{2}/2}\,e^{t^{2}/2}\,dx=\exp\!\left(\frac{t^{2}}{2}\right).

≤M8​(ck02dk0−2​ϵdk0)+O​(ϵ2)<M8​ck02dk0=M8​∑k≠0ck2dk=ℰ\displaystyle\leq\frac{M}{8}\left(\frac{c_{k_{0}}^{2}}{d_{k_{0}}}-\frac{2\epsilon}{d_{k_{0}}}\right)+O(\epsilon^{2})<\frac{M}{8}\frac{c_{k_{0}}^{2}}{d_{k_{0}}}=\frac{M}{8}\sum_{k\neq 0}\frac{c_{k}^{2}}{d_{k}}=\mathcal{E} (24)

Optimizing in Real domain. The above analysis uses complex irreducible representations. For real 𝐰\mathbf{w}, S^k,r\hat{S}_{k,r} will be a complex conjugate of S^−k,r\hat{S}_{-k,r} for conjugate irreducible representations kk and −k-k. This means that we can partition the sum in Eqn. 20 into real and complex parts:

ℰ​(𝐰)=M2​∑k≠0,k​real1dk​|∑rtr⁡(S^k,r)|2+M​∑k≠0,k​complex,take​one1dk​|∑rtr⁡(S^k,r)|2\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{w})=\frac{M}{2}\sum_{k\neq 0,k\ \mathrm{real}}\frac{1}{d_{k}}\Big|\sum_{r}\operatorname{tr}(\hat{S}_{k,r})\Big|^{2}+M\sum_{k\neq 0,k\ \mathrm{complex,\ take\ one}}\frac{1}{d_{k}}\Big|\sum_{r}\operatorname{tr}(\hat{S}_{k,r})\Big|^{2} (25)

The above equation holds since RgR_{g} is real, and for any complex irreducible representation kk, its conjugate representation −k-k is also included. Therefore, to optimize ℰ\mathcal{E} in the real domain ℝ\mathbb{R}, we can just optimize only on the real part plus the complex part taken one of the conjugate pair in the complex domain ℂ\mathbb{C}.

Zero-meaned one hot representation. Note that if we use zero-meaned one hot representation 𝐞~h=P1⟂​𝐞h\tilde{\mathbf{e}}_{h}=P^{\perp}_{1}\mathbf{e}_{h}, then Rh1​𝐞~h2=𝐞~h1​h2R_{h_{1}}\tilde{\mathbf{e}}_{h_{2}}=\tilde{\mathbf{e}}_{h_{1}h_{2}} and P​𝐞~h=𝐞~h−1P\tilde{\mathbf{e}}_{h}=\tilde{\mathbf{e}}_{h^{-1}} still hold, and X~h=P1⟂​Xh=P1⟂​[Rh⊤,P]=[Rh⊤,P]​[P1⟂;P1⟂]\tilde{X}_{h}=P^{\perp}_{1}X_{h}=P^{\perp}_{1}[R^{\top}_{h},P]=[R^{\top}_{h},P][P^{\perp}_{1};P^{\perp}_{1}]. This means that we can still use XhX_{h} but enforce zero-meaned constraints on 𝐮\mathbf{u} and 𝐯\mathbf{v}, which is already included since Q∗​𝟏=0Q^{*}\mathbf{1}=0.

See 1

Proof.

For Abelian group HH with |H|=M>2|H|=M>2, all irreducible representations are 1-dimensional, and at least one of it is complex. Since ℂ\mathbb{C} is treated as 2D space in optimization, it has at least 1 degree of freedom to change without changing its function value (Eqn. 25). So the Hessian has at least 1 zero eigenvalue. For non-Abelian group, there is at least one irreducible representation kk with dimension greater than 1, which means it has at least 1 degrees of freedom to change S^k,r\hat{S}_{k,r} without changing |∑rtr⁡(S^k,r)|2|\sum_{r}\operatorname{tr}(\hat{S}_{k,r})|^{2} and thus its function value (Eqn. 25). So the Hessian has at least 1 zero eigenvalue. ∎

A.2 Reconstruction power of learned features (Sec. 4.4)

Proof.

For each nontrivial irrep kk, let Πk\Pi_{k} be the central idempotent projector onto the isotypic subspace ℋk=Imk⊗ℂdk\mathcal{H}_{k}=I_{m_{k}}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{d_{k}} (for the regular rep, mk=dkm_{k}=d_{k}). Let End​(ℋk)\mathrm{End}(\mathcal{H}_{k}) be the space of all linear operators that map ℋk\mathcal{H}_{k} to itself. Note that the dimensionality of ℋk\mathcal{H}_{k} is Dk:=mk​dkD_{k}:=m_{k}d_{k}.

Let 𝐰j=[𝐮j,P​𝐯j]\mathbf{w}_{j}=[\mathbf{u}_{j},P\mathbf{v}_{j}] be the weights learned by optimizing the energy function ℰ\mathcal{E} with quadratic activation σ​(x)=x2\sigma(x)=x^{2}. From Thm. 2, we know that at local optima, 𝐮j=±𝐯j\mathbf{u}_{j}=\pm\mathbf{v}_{j} and 𝟏⊤​𝐮j=0\mathbf{1}^{\top}\mathbf{u}_{j}=0. Therefore, the feature 𝐟~j,h∈ℝM\tilde{\mathbf{f}}_{j,h}\in\mathbb{R}^{M} is given by (∘\circ denotes the Hadamard product)

𝐟~j,h=±2​(Rh⊤​𝐮j)∘𝐮j+(Rh⊤​𝐮j)∘2−1M​∑h(Rh⊤​𝐮j)∘2\tilde{\mathbf{f}}_{j,h}=\pm 2\,(R_{h}^{\top}\mathbf{u}_{j})\circ\mathbf{u}_{j}+(R_{h}^{\top}\mathbf{u}_{j})^{\circ 2}-\frac{1}{M}\sum_{h}(R_{h}^{\top}\mathbf{u}_{j})^{\circ 2}

The third term 𝐮∘2\mathbf{u}^{\circ 2} is a constant across all hh and was removed in the zero-meaned projection. By our assumption we have node jj and j′j^{\prime} with both positive and negative signs. So 12​(𝐟~j,h−𝐟~j′,h)=2​(Rh⊤​𝐮j)∘𝐮j\frac{1}{2}\left(\tilde{\mathbf{f}}_{j,h}-\tilde{\mathbf{f}}_{j^{\prime},h}\right)=2\,(R_{h}^{\top}\mathbf{u}_{j})\circ\mathbf{u}_{j}. If a linear representation of {𝐟~j}\{\tilde{\mathbf{f}}_{j}\} can perfectly reconstruct the target Y~\tilde{Y}, so does the original representation. So for now we just let feature 𝐟~j,h=2​(Rh⊤​𝐮j)∘𝐮j=2​diag​(Rh⊤​𝐮j​𝐮j∗)\tilde{\mathbf{f}}_{j,h}=2\,(R_{h}^{\top}\mathbf{u}_{j})\circ\mathbf{u}_{j}=2\text{diag}(R_{h}^{\top}\mathbf{u}_{j}\mathbf{u}_{j}^{\ast}). Let Uj:=𝐮j​𝐮j∗U_{j}:=\mathbf{u}_{j}\mathbf{u}_{j}^{\ast}, which is Hermitian in End​(ℋk)\mathrm{End}(\mathcal{H}_{k}), then 𝐟~j,h=2​diag​(Rh⊤​Uj)\tilde{\mathbf{f}}_{j,h}=2\text{diag}(R_{h}^{\top}U_{j}).

Gram block diagonalization. For each irrep kk, let JkJ_{k} be the set of all node jj that converges to the kk-th irrep. For any Hermitian operator UU supported in ℋk\mathcal{H}_{k} (i.e. U=Πk​U​ΠkU=\Pi_{k}U\Pi_{k}), define the centered quadratic cross-feature

𝐜U​(h):= 2​diag​(Rh⊤​U)∈ℂM,\mathbf{c}_{U}(h)\ :=\ 2\,\text{diag}(R_{h}^{\top}U)\in\mathbb{C}^{M},

Property of the square term. With quadratic features the class-centered column for node jj and block hh decomposes as F~=[A,B]\tilde{F}=[A,B], where for BB each column jj (and block hh) is 𝐛j,h:=Rh⊤​(𝐮j∘2)−‖𝐮j‖22M​𝟏M\mathbf{b}_{j,h}:=R_{h}^{\top}(\mathbf{u}_{j}^{\circ 2})-\tfrac{\|\mathbf{u}_{j}\|_{2}^{2}}{M}\mathbf{1}_{M} (the “square” part) and for AA each column jj (and block hh) is 𝐚j,h:=2​(Rh⊤​𝐮j)∘𝐮j\mathbf{a}_{j,h}:=2\,(R_{h}^{\top}\mathbf{u}_{j})\circ\mathbf{u}_{j} (the “cross” part we discussed above). where we used χk​(a)¯=χk​(a−1)\overline{\chi_{k}(a)}=\chi_{k}(a^{-1}) for unitary irreps. Consequently,

ℰ𝒮=12​‖(Φ𝒮⊗𝟏M)∗​F‖22=12​‖Φ𝒮∗​𝐳‖22\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{S}}=\frac{1}{2}\|(\Phi_{\mathcal{S}}\otimes\mathbf{1}_{M})^{\ast}F\|_{2}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\|\Phi_{\mathcal{S}}^{\ast}\mathbf{z}\|_{2}^{2}

[Φ𝒮∗​𝐳]k=⟨∑h∈HdkM​χk​(h)¯​Rh,S⟩=Mdk​⟨Πk,S⟩[\Phi_{\mathcal{S}}^{\ast}\mathbf{z}]_{k}=\langle\sum_{h\in H}\sqrt{\frac{d_{k}}{M}}\overline{\chi_{k}(h)}R_{h},S\rangle=\sqrt{\frac{M}{d_{k}}}\langle\Pi_{k},S\rangle

In the QQ space, we have ⟨Πk,S⟩=∑r=1mktr⁡(S^k,r)\langle\Pi_{k},S\rangle=\sum_{r=1}^{m_{k}}\operatorname{tr}(\hat{S}_{k,r}) and therefore

ℰ𝒮=12​∑k≠0,k∉𝒮Mdk​|⟨Πk,S⟩|2=M2​∑k≠0,k∉𝒮1dk​|∑rtr⁡(S^k,r)|2\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{S}}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k\neq 0,k\notin\mathcal{S}}\frac{M}{d_{k}}\big|\langle\Pi_{k},S\rangle\big|^{2}=\frac{M}{2}\sum_{k\neq 0,k\notin\mathcal{S}}\frac{1}{d_{k}}\Big|\sum_{r}\operatorname{tr}(\hat{S}_{k,r})\Big|^{2}

which is exactly the same form as the decomposition (Eqn. 20) in Thm. 2 (but a much cleaner derivation). Therefore, all the local maxima of ℰ𝒮\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{S}} are still in the same form as Thm. 2, but we just remove those local maxima that are in isotype/irreps k∈𝒮k\in\mathcal{S}, and focus on missing ones. ∎

B.3 Muon optimizers lead to diversity (Sec. 5.3)

Proof.

Let G=[∇𝐰1ℰ,∇𝐰2ℰ,…,∇𝐰Kℰ]G=[\nabla_{\mathbf{w}_{1}}\mathcal{E},\nabla_{\mathbf{w}_{2}}\mathcal{E},\ldots,\nabla_{\mathbf{w}_{K}}\mathcal{E}] be the gradient matrix. Let G=U​D​V⊤G=UDV^{\top} be the singular value decomposition. Then Muon direction is G^=U​V⊤\hat{G}=UV^{\top} and thus the inner product between G^\hat{G} and GG is

⟨G^,G⟩F=tr⁡(G^⊤​G)=tr⁡(V​U⊤​U​D​V⊤)=tr⁡(D)≥0\langle\hat{G},G\rangle_{F}=\operatorname{tr}(\hat{G}^{\top}G)=\operatorname{tr}(VU^{\top}UDV^{\top})=\operatorname{tr}(D)\geq 0 (36)

So Muon always follows the gradient direction and improve the objective. Furthermore, ⟨G^,G⟩F=0\langle\hat{G},G\rangle_{F}=0 iff D=0D=0, which means that G=0G=0. So the stationary points of the Muon dynamics and the original gradient dynamics are identical. ∎

Lemma 7 (Proposition of Fréchet / log-Gumbel selection).

Let x1,…,xnx_{1},\dots,x_{n} be i.i.d. positive random variables with Fréchet(α\alpha) CDF

F​(x)=exp⁡(−x−α),x>0,α>0,F(x)=\exp\!\big(-x^{-\alpha}\big),\qquad x>0,\ \ \alpha>0,

and let w1,…,wn>0w_{1},\dots,w_{n}>0 be fixed weights. Define

i∗=arg⁡max1≤j≤n⁡wj​xj.i^{*}\;=\;\arg\max_{1\leq j\leq n}\;w_{j}\,x_{j}.

Then

Pr(i∗=i)=wiα∑j=1nwjα,i=1,…,n.\boxed{\quad\Pr\big(i^{*}=i\big)\;=\;\dfrac{w_{i}^{\alpha}}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_{j}^{\alpha}}\,,\qquad i=1,\dots,n.\quad}

In particular, when α=1\alpha=1,

Pr(i∗=i)=wi∑j=1nwj.\boxed{\quad\Pr\big(i^{*}=i\big)\;=\;\dfrac{w_{i}}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_{j}}\,.\quad}
Proof.

Set Yj:=wj​xjY_{j}:=w_{j}x_{j}. For t>0t>0,

Pr⁡(maxj⁡Yj≤t)=∏j=1nF​(twj)=exp⁡(−∑j=1n(wj/t)α).\Pr\!\big(\max_{j}Y_{j}\leq t\big)=\prod_{j=1}^{n}F\!\Big(\frac{t}{w_{j}}\Big)=\exp\!\Big(-\sum_{j=1}^{n}(w_{j}/t)^{\alpha}\Big).

Differentiating gives the density of the maximum:

fmax​(t)=dd​t​Pr⁡(maxj⁡Yj≤t)=(∑j=1nα​wjα​t−α−1)​exp⁡(−∑j=1n(wj/t)α).f_{\max}(t)=\frac{d}{dt}\Pr\!\big(\max_{j}Y_{j}\leq t\big)=\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{n}\alpha\,w_{j}^{\alpha}\,t^{-\alpha-1}\Big)\,\exp\!\Big(-\sum_{j=1}^{n}(w_{j}/t)^{\alpha}\Big).

The density that “ii achieves the maximum at level tt” is

fYi​(t)​∏j≠iF​(twj)=α​wiα​t−α−1​exp⁡(−∑j=1n(wj/t)α).f_{Y_{i}}(t)\,\prod_{j\neq i}F\!\Big(\frac{t}{w_{j}}\Big)=\alpha\,w_{i}^{\alpha}\,t^{-\alpha-1}\,\exp\!\Big(-\sum_{j=1}^{n}(w_{j}/t)^{\alpha}\Big).

Hence the conditional probability that ii is the argmax given maxj⁡Yj=t\max_{j}Y_{j}=t is

Pr⁡(i∗=i∣maxj⁡Yj=t)=α​wiα​t−α−1∑j=1nα​wjα​t−α−1=wiα∑j=1nwjα,\Pr\!\big(i^{*}=i\mid\max_{j}Y_{j}=t\big)=\frac{\alpha\,w_{i}^{\alpha}\,t^{-\alpha-1}}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}\alpha\,w_{j}^{\alpha}\,t^{-\alpha-1}}=\frac{w_{i}^{\alpha}}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_{j}^{\alpha}},

which is independent of tt. Averaging over tt yields the stated result. ∎

with the constraint ∑j=1Lαj2≤1\sum_{j=1}^{L}\alpha_{j}^{2}\leq 1. Define

rj:=μj​αj.r_{j}:=\mu_{j}\alpha_{j}.

Interior. In the interior, we have

For any pair i,ki,k define the ratio

ρi​k:=rirk.\rho_{ik}:=\frac{r_{i}}{r_{k}}.

Its derivative is

dd​t​log⁡rirk=ri−rk.\frac{d}{dt}\log\frac{r_{i}}{r_{k}}=r_{i}-r_{k}.

Thus if rℓ​(0)>rj​(0)r_{\ell}(0)>r_{j}(0), then dd​t​log⁡(rℓ/rj)>0\frac{d}{dt}\log(r_{\ell}/r_{j})>0 and ρℓ​j​(t)\rho_{\ell j}(t) is strictly increasing. Hence a strict leader in rr cannot be overtaken in the interior.

Boundary region (∑jαj2=1\sum_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}=1). On the unit sphere, the projected dynamics is

α˙j=μj​αj2−λ​αj,λ=∑k=1Lμk​αk3.\dot{\alpha}_{j}=\mu_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2}-\lambda\alpha_{j},\qquad\lambda=\sum_{k=1}^{L}\mu_{k}\alpha_{k}^{3}.

In terms of rjr_{j},

For the ratio ρi​k=ri/rk\rho_{ik}=r_{i}/r_{k} we again obtain

implying wℓ​(t)→1w_{\ell}(t)\to 1 and wj​(t)→0w_{j}(t)\to 0. Hence

Lemma 9 (Muon projection).

For the matrix A=[Q,𝐯]A=[Q,\mathbf{v}] where QQ is a column orthonormal matrix and 𝐯\mathbf{v} is a vector with small magnitude, its Muon regulated version A^=[A^1,𝐯^]\hat{A}=[\hat{A}_{1},\hat{\mathbf{v}}] takes the following form:

where 𝐯∥=Q​Q⊤​𝐯\mathbf{v}_{\parallel}=QQ^{\top}\mathbf{v} and 𝐯⟂=I−Q​Q⊤​𝐯\mathbf{v}_{\perp}=I-QQ^{\top}\mathbf{v}.

A^(c)=A​(A⊤​A)−1/c,A^(c)=[A^1(c),A^2(c)].\widehat{A}^{(c)}\;=\;A\,(A^{\top}A)^{-1/c},\qquad\widehat{A}^{(c)}=\big[\widehat{A}^{(c)}_{1},\ \widehat{A}^{(c)}_{2}\big].

We derive a first-order (in CC) formula for the last block A^2(c)\widehat{A}^{(c)}_{2}.

The exact Gram matrix is

G:=A⊤​A=[IkCC⊤C⊤​C+T]=G0+H,G0:=diag​(Ik,T),H:=[0CC⊤C⊤​C].G:=A^{\top}A=\begin{bmatrix}I_{k}&C\\ C^{\top}&C^{\top}C+T\end{bmatrix}=G_{0}+H,\qquad G_{0}:=\mathrm{diag}(I_{k},T),\quad H:=\begin{bmatrix}0&C\\ C^{\top}&C^{\top}C\end{bmatrix}.

Treat CC as small. To first order in CC we may drop the quadratic block:

H=[0CC⊤0]+O​(‖C‖2).H\;=\;\begin{bmatrix}0&C\\ C^{\top}&0\end{bmatrix}\;+\;O(\|C\|^{2}).

Diagonalizing TT. Let T=U​Λ​U⊤T=U\Lambda U^{\top} with Λ=diag​(λ1,…,λm)\Lambda=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{m}), λj>0\lambda_{j}>0. Define the block orthogonal change of basis

P:=diag​(Ik,U)⇒G~:=P⊤​G​P,G~0:=P⊤​G0​P=diag​(Ik,Λ),H~:=P⊤​H​P=[0C~C~⊤0],P:=\mathrm{diag}(I_{k},\,U)\quad\Rightarrow\quad\widetilde{G}:=P^{\top}GP,\quad\widetilde{G}_{0}:=P^{\top}G_{0}P=\mathrm{diag}(I_{k},\Lambda),\quad\widetilde{H}:=P^{\top}HP=\begin{bmatrix}0&\widetilde{C}\\ \widetilde{C}^{\top}&0\end{bmatrix},

where C~:=C​U\widetilde{C}:=C\,U. All first-order statements can be done in this basis and then mapped back by PP.

G~=G~0+H~=G~01/2​(I+G~0−1/2​H~​G~0−1/2⏟=⁣:E)​G~01/2.\widetilde{G}=\widetilde{G}_{0}+\widetilde{H}=\widetilde{G}_{0}^{1/2}\Big(I+\underbrace{\widetilde{G}_{0}^{-1/2}\,\widetilde{H}\,\widetilde{G}_{0}^{-1/2}}_{=:E}\Big)\widetilde{G}_{0}^{1/2}.

Since G~0=diag​(Ik,Λ)\widetilde{G}_{0}=\mathrm{diag}(I_{k},\Lambda),

For the scalar function f​(x)=x−1/cf(x)=x^{-1/c},

G~0−1/2​E​G~0−1/2=[0C~​Λ−1Λ−1​C~⊤0].\widetilde{G}_{0}^{-1/2}E\,\widetilde{G}_{0}^{-1/2}=\begin{bmatrix}0&\widetilde{C}\,\Lambda^{-1}\\ \Lambda^{-1}\widetilde{C}^{\top}&0\end{bmatrix}.

Since U​Λ−1​U⊤=T−1U\,\Lambda^{-1}U^{\top}=T^{-1} and U​Λ−1/c​U⊤=T−1/cU\,\Lambda^{-1/c}U^{\top}=T^{-1/c},

G−1/c=[Ik00T−1/c]−1c​[0C​T−1T−1​C⊤0]+O​(‖C‖2).G^{-1/c}=\begin{bmatrix}I_{k}&0\\[2.0pt] 0&T^{-1/c}\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{c}\begin{bmatrix}0&C\,T^{-1}\\[2.0pt] T^{-1}C^{\top}&0\end{bmatrix}\;+\;O(\|C\|^{2}).

and we have

Independent feature learning. In this case, getting all local modes {𝜻l}\{\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{l}\} is identical to the coupon collector problem with LL coupons. With the property of the distribution (Lemma 7), we know that the probability of getting ll-th local maxima is pl:=μla/∑lμlap_{l}:=\mu_{l}^{a}/\sum_{l}\mu_{l}^{a}.

Therefore, the expected number of trials to collect all local maxima is (Flajolet et al., 1992):

Muon guiding. Consider the following setting that we optimize the hidden nodes “incrementally”. When learning the weights of node jj, we assume all the previous nodes (node 11 to node j−1j-1) have been learned, i.e., they have converged to one of the ground truth bases {𝜻l}\{\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{l}\}, but still keep the gradients of them (after deduplication) in the Muon update. Appendix C More detailed analysis On stage I (Lazy Learning)

To analyze the Stage I more thoroughly, we consider the gradient-flow dynamics of the output layer weights VV.

Let F~∈ℝn×K\tilde{F}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times K} be a fixed feature matrix and Y~∈ℝn×M\tilde{Y}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times M}.

We assume throughout that

  • (A1)

    F~\tilde{F} has full column rank KK, and

  • (A2)

    col​(Y~)⊆col​(F~)\mathrm{col}(\tilde{Y})\subseteq\mathrm{col}(\tilde{F}), i.e. there exists V⋆∈ℝK×MV^{\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times M} such that Y~=F~​V⋆\tilde{Y}=\tilde{F}V^{\star}.

  • (A3)

    Small and independent random initialization on entries of V​(0)V(0), with mean zero and variance α2\alpha^{2}, where 0<α≪10<\alpha\ll 1, and thus ‖V​(0)‖F=O​(α​K​M)\|V(0)\|_{F}=O(\alpha\sqrt{KM}) with high probability.

  • (A4)

Note that (A4) is optional. It simplifies some interpretations but is not needed for the main analysis.

We train a linear readout V∈ℝK×MV\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times M} by minimizing

J​(V)=12​(‖Y~−F~​V‖F2+η​‖V‖F2),η≥0.J(V)\;=\;\frac{1}{2}\bigl(\|\tilde{Y}-\tilde{F}V\|_{F}^{2}+\eta\|V\|_{F}^{2}\bigr),\qquad\eta\geq 0. (47)

E​(t):=Y~−F~​V​(t)∈ℝn×M,GF~​(t):=E​(t)​V​(t)⊤∈ℝn×K.E(t):=\tilde{Y}-\tilde{F}V(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times M},\qquad G_{\tilde{F}}(t):=E(t)V(t)^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times K}. (48)

because 𝟏⊤​F~=0\mathbf{1}^{\top}\tilde{F}=0 and 𝟏⊤​Y~=0\mathbf{1}^{\top}\tilde{Y}=0.

C.1.2 Why Y~​Y~⊤​F~\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}\tilde{F} is the leading term

We now compare the deterministic term Y~​Y~⊤​F~\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}\tilde{F} to the V0V_{0}–dependent terms using norm inequalities.

Lemma 11 (Lower bound on ‖Y~​Y~⊤​F~‖F\|\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}\tilde{F}\|_{F}).

Let F~\tilde{F} have full column rank and Y~\tilde{Y} be nonzero. Then

‖Y~​Y~⊤​F~‖F≥σmin​(F~)​‖Y~​Y~⊤‖F>0,\|\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}\tilde{F}\|_{F}\;\geq\;\sigma_{\min}(\tilde{F})\,\|\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}\|_{F}>0,

where σmin​(F~)\sigma_{\min}(\tilde{F}) is the smallest singular value of F~\tilde{F}.

Proof.

For any matrices A,BA,B, ‖A​B‖F2=tr⁡(B​B⊤​A⊤​A)\|AB\|_{F}^{2}=\operatorname{tr}(BB^{\top}A^{\top}A). Take A=Y~​Y~⊤A=\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}, B=F~B=\tilde{F}. Since B​B⊤BB^{\top} is PSD with eigenvalues bounded below by σmin​(F~)2\sigma_{\min}(\tilde{F})^{2},

‖A​B‖F2=tr⁡(B​B⊤​A⊤​A)≥σmin​(F~)2​tr⁡(A⊤​A)=σmin​(F~)2​‖A‖F2.\|AB\|_{F}^{2}=\operatorname{tr}(BB^{\top}A^{\top}A)\geq\sigma_{\min}(\tilde{F})^{2}\,\operatorname{tr}(A^{\top}A)=\sigma_{\min}(\tilde{F})^{2}\|A\|_{F}^{2}.

Taking square roots gives the result. ∎

Next, bound the V0V_{0}–dependent part. For concreteness, consider the term F~​F~⊤​Y~​V0⊤\tilde{F}\tilde{F}^{\top}\tilde{Y}V_{0}^{\top} (other mixed terms are bounded similarly). Using ‖A​B‖F≤‖A‖F​‖B‖F\|AB\|_{F}\leq\|A\|_{F}\|B\|_{F},

‖F~​F~⊤​Y~​V0⊤‖F≤‖F~​F~⊤​Y~‖F​‖V0‖F.\|\tilde{F}\tilde{F}^{\top}\tilde{Y}V_{0}^{\top}\|_{F}\;\leq\;\|\tilde{F}\tilde{F}^{\top}\tilde{Y}\|_{F}\|V_{0}\|_{F}.

Under the iid initialization with variance α2\alpha^{2}, ‖V0‖F=O​(α​K​M)\|V_{0}\|_{F}=O(\alpha\sqrt{KM}), hence

‖F~​F~⊤​Y~​V0⊤‖F=O​(α).\|\tilde{F}\tilde{F}^{\top}\tilde{Y}V_{0}^{\top}\|_{F}=O(\alpha).

The same argument applies to all other V0V_{0}–dependent order–tt terms in R1​(V0)R_{1}(V_{0}).

Combining Lemma 11 with these upper bounds yields

‖R1​(V0)‖F‖Y~​Y~⊤​F~‖F≤C​(F~,Y~,K,M)​α\frac{\|R_{1}(V_{0})\|_{F}}{\|\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}\tilde{F}\|_{F}}\;\leq\;C(\tilde{F},\tilde{Y},K,M)\,\alpha

for some constant CC independent of α\alpha. Thus, in the limit α→0\alpha\to 0 (small random initialization), the term Y~​Y~⊤​F~\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}\tilde{F} is the unique leading contribution at order tt.

Proposition 2 (Small–time leading term of GF~G_{\tilde{F}}).

Under assumptions (A1)–(A2) and small random initialization with scale α≪1\alpha\ll 1,

GF~​(t)=Y~​V0⊤+t​Y~​Y~⊤​F~+O​(t​α+t2)G_{\tilde{F}}(t)=\tilde{Y}V_{0}^{\top}+t\,\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}\tilde{F}+O\bigl(t\alpha+t^{2}\bigr)

in Frobenius norm. In particular, as α→0\alpha\to 0,

GF~​(t)−Y~​V0⊤t→Y~​Y~⊤​F~,and‖GF~​(t)‖F∼t​‖Y~​Y~⊤​F~‖F\frac{G_{\tilde{F}}(t)-\tilde{Y}V_{0}^{\top}}{t}\;\to\;\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}\tilde{F},\qquad\text{and}\qquad\|G_{\tilde{F}}(t)\|_{F}\sim t\,\|\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}\tilde{F}\|_{F}

for fixed small tt, independently of whether η=0\eta=0 or η>0\eta>0.

The weight decay parameter η\eta only appears in products involving V0V_{0}, and hence all η\eta–dependent order–tt contributions are also O​(α)O(\alpha) in norm. Therefore the leading deterministic term Y~​Y~⊤​F~\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}\tilde{F} is the same for both η=0\eta=0 and η>0\eta>0.

C.2 Long–time decay of GF~G_{\tilde{F}}

We now analyze the behavior of GF~​(t)G_{\tilde{F}}(t) as t→∞t\to\infty, again for both η=0\eta=0 and η>0\eta>0.

C.2.1 General solution of the gradient flow

From (52), the gradient flow is a linear ODE with constant coefficients. The unique fixed point V⋆V^{\star} satisfies

A​V⋆=B⇒V⋆=A−1​B.AV^{\star}=B\quad\Rightarrow\quad V^{\star}=A^{-1}B.

Define Δ​V​(t):=V​(t)−V⋆\Delta V(t):=V(t)-V^{\star}. Then

dd​t​Δ​V​(t)=−A​Δ​V​(t),Δ​V​(t)=e−A​t​Δ​V​(0),\frac{d}{dt}\Delta V(t)=-A\Delta V(t),\qquad\Delta V(t)=e^{-At}\Delta V(0),

and hence

V​(t)=e−A​t​(V​(0)−V⋆)+V⋆.V(t)=e^{-At}(V(0)-V^{\star})+V^{\star}. (56)

Let λmin​(A)\lambda_{\min}(A) denote the smallest eigenvalue of AA. Since A⪰F~⊤​F~A\succeq\tilde{F}^{\top}\tilde{F} and F~\tilde{F} has full column rank, λmin​(A)≥σmin​(F~)2\lambda_{\min}(A)\geq\sigma_{\min}(\tilde{F})^{2} for η=0\eta=0 and λmin​(A)≥σmin​(F~)2+η\lambda_{\min}(A)\geq\sigma_{\min}(\tilde{F})^{2}+\eta for η>0\eta>0. Standard bounds on matrix exponentials give

‖Δ​V​(t)‖F≤e−λmin​(A)​t​‖Δ​V​(0)‖F.\|\Delta V(t)\|_{F}\leq e^{-\lambda_{\min}(A)t}\,\|\Delta V(0)\|_{F}. (57)

The error satisfies

E(t)=Y~−F~V(t)=Y~−F~V⋆−F~ΔV(t)=:E⋆−F~ΔV(t),E(t)=\tilde{Y}-\tilde{F}V(t)=\tilde{Y}-\tilde{F}V^{\star}-\tilde{F}\Delta V(t)=:E^{\star}-\tilde{F}\Delta V(t),

where E⋆:=Y~−F~​V⋆E^{\star}:=\tilde{Y}-\tilde{F}V^{\star} is the residual at the minimizer. Using ‖F~​Δ​V​(t)‖F≤‖F~‖2​‖Δ​V​(t)‖F\|\tilde{F}\Delta V(t)\|_{F}\leq\|\tilde{F}\|_{2}\|\Delta V(t)\|_{F} and (57),

‖E​(t)−E⋆‖F≤‖F~‖2​e−λmin​(A)​t​‖Δ​V​(0)‖F.\|E(t)-E^{\star}\|_{F}\leq\|\tilde{F}\|_{2}\,e^{-\lambda_{\min}(A)t}\,\|\Delta V(0)\|_{F}. (58)

C.2.2 Case η=0\eta=0

When η=0\eta=0, we have A=F~⊤​F~A=\tilde{F}^{\top}\tilde{F}. By assumption (A2), Y~=F~​V⋆\tilde{Y}=\tilde{F}V^{\star} is exactly realized by the model, so E⋆=0E^{\star}=0, i.e.

limt→∞E​(t)=0.\lim_{t\to\infty}E(t)=0.

Equations (57) and (58) imply exponential decay:

‖V​(t)−V⋆‖F≤e−σmin​(F~)2​t​‖V​(0)−V⋆‖F,‖E​(t)‖F≤‖F~‖2​e−σmin​(F~)2​t​‖V​(0)−V⋆‖F.\|V(t)-V^{\star}\|_{F}\leq e^{-\sigma_{\min}(\tilde{F})^{2}t}\,\|V(0)-V^{\star}\|_{F},\qquad\|E(t)\|_{F}\leq\|\tilde{F}\|_{2}e^{-\sigma_{\min}(\tilde{F})^{2}t}\,\|V(0)-V^{\star}\|_{F}.

GF~​(t)=E​(t)​V​(t)⊤,G_{\tilde{F}}(t)=E(t)V(t)^{\top},

‖GF~​(t)‖F≤‖E​(t)‖F​‖V​(t)‖2≤‖E​(t)‖F​(‖V⋆‖2+‖V​(t)−V⋆‖2).\|G_{\tilde{F}}(t)\|_{F}\leq\|E(t)\|_{F}\,\|V(t)\|_{2}\leq\|E(t)\|_{F}\,\bigl(\|V^{\star}\|_{2}+\|V(t)-V^{\star}\|_{2}\bigr). (59)

Using the exponential bounds above and the fact that ‖V​(t)−V⋆‖2≤‖V​(t)−V⋆‖F\|V(t)-V^{\star}\|_{2}\leq\|V(t)-V^{\star}\|_{F}, we obtain

‖GF~​(t)‖F≤C0​e−σmin​(F~)2​t\|G_{\tilde{F}}(t)\|_{F}\leq C_{0}\,e^{-\sigma_{\min}(\tilde{F})^{2}t}

Thus in the realizable, unregularized case, the backpropagated gradient decays exponentially to zero.

Proposition 3 (Exponential decay of GF~G_{\tilde{F}} for η=0\eta=0).

Assume (A1)–(A2) and η=0\eta=0. Then

limt→∞GF~​(t)=0,\lim_{t\to\infty}G_{\tilde{F}}(t)=0,

and there exists C0>0C_{0}>0 such that

‖GF~​(t)‖F≤C0​e−σmin​(F~)2​tfor all ​t≥0.\|G_{\tilde{F}}(t)\|_{F}\leq C_{0}\,e^{-\sigma_{\min}(\tilde{F})^{2}t}\qquad\text{for all }t\geq 0.

A more refined analysis using the SVD F~=U​Σ​W⊤\tilde{F}=U\Sigma W^{\top} shows that every singular direction of GF~​(t)G_{\tilde{F}}(t) is a finite linear combination of exponentials e−(σi2+σi′2)​te^{-(\sigma_{i}^{2}+\sigma_{i^{\prime}}^{2})t} and e−σi2​te^{-\sigma_{i}^{2}t}, so the slowest rate in the Frobenius norm is indeed e−σmin​(F~)2​te^{-\sigma_{\min}(\tilde{F})^{2}t}.

When η>0\eta>0, the minimizer V⋆=A−1​F~⊤​Y~V^{\star}=A^{-1}\tilde{F}^{\top}\tilde{Y} is the ridge solution. In general it does not exactly interpolate Y~\tilde{Y}, and the residual

To study the convergence, write

‖GF~​(t)−GF~⋆‖F\displaystyle\|G_{\tilde{F}}(t)-G_{\tilde{F}}^{\star}\|_{F} ≤‖E​(t)−E⋆‖F​‖V​(t)‖2+‖E⋆‖F​‖V​(t)−V⋆‖2\displaystyle\leq\|E(t)-E^{\star}\|_{F}\,\|V(t)\|_{2}+\|E^{\star}\|_{F}\,\|V(t)-V^{\star}\|_{2}

Proposition 4 (Exponential convergence of GF~G_{\tilde{F}} for η>0\eta>0).

Assume (A1)–(A2) and η>0\eta>0. Then

limt→∞GF~​(t)=GF~⋆:=E⋆​V⋆⊤≠0​ in general,\lim_{t\to\infty}G_{\tilde{F}}(t)=G_{\tilde{F}}^{\star}:=E^{\star}V^{\star\top}\neq 0\ \text{ in general},

and there exists C1>0C_{1}>0 such that

‖GF~​(t)−GF~⋆‖F≤C1​e−λmin​(A)​t,λmin​(A)≥σmin​(F~)2+η.\|G_{\tilde{F}}(t)-G_{\tilde{F}}^{\star}\|_{F}\leq C_{1}\,e^{-\lambda_{\min}(A)t},\qquad\lambda_{\min}(A)\;\geq\;\sigma_{\min}(\tilde{F})^{2}+\eta.

Finally, note that

GF~⋆=E⋆​V⋆⊤=Pη​Y~​V⋆⊤=η​(F~​F~⊤+η​I)−1​Y~​Y~⊤​F~​(F~⊤​F~+η​I)−1G^{\star}_{\tilde{F}}=E^{\star}V^{\star\top}=P_{\eta}\tilde{Y}V^{\star\top}=\eta(\tilde{F}\tilde{F}^{\top}+\eta I)^{-1}\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}\tilde{F}(\tilde{F}^{\top}\tilde{F}+\eta I)^{-1} (60)

where Pη:=I−F~​(F~⊤​F~+η​I)−1​F~⊤=η​(F~​F~⊤+η​I)−1P_{\eta}:=I-\tilde{F}(\tilde{F}^{\top}\tilde{F}+\eta I)^{-1}\tilde{F}^{\top}=\eta(\tilde{F}\tilde{F}^{\top}+\eta I)^{-1}, by Woodbury matrix formula.

Summary.

  • •

    For small tt, the leading term in GF~​(t)G_{\tilde{F}}(t) is t​Y~​Y~⊤​F~t\,\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}\tilde{F}, independent of η\eta. All other terms (including those involving V​(0)V(0) and η\eta) are lower order in the initialization scale α\alpha.

C.3 Scaling the network output by β\beta

We now modify the objective by inserting a scalar factor β>0\beta>0 on the network output:

J​(V)=12​‖Y~−β​F~​V‖F2,F~∈ℝn×K,Y~∈ℝn×M,V∈ℝK×M.J(V)\;=\;\frac{1}{2}\bigl\|\tilde{Y}-\beta\tilde{F}V\bigr\|_{F}^{2},\qquad\tilde{F}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times K},\ \tilde{Y}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times M},\ V\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times M}. (61)

We study the gradient flow dynamics for VV and, in particular, the initial behavior of the backpropagated gradient on F~\tilde{F},

GF~​(t):=E​(t)​V​(t)⊤,E​(t):=Y~−β​F~​V​(t).G_{\tilde{F}}(t):=E(t)V(t)^{\top},\qquad E(t):=\tilde{Y}-\beta\tilde{F}V(t).

Appendix D More Experiments

D.1 Use Groups Algorithms Programming (GAP) to get non-Abelian groups

GAP (https://www.gap-system.org/) is a programming language with a library of thousands of functions to create and manipulate group. Using GAP, one can easily enumerate all non-abelian group of size M≤127M\leq 127 and create their multiplication tables, which is what we have done here. From these non-Abelian groups, for each group size MM, we pick one for our scaling law experiments (Fig. 5 bottom right) with maxk⁡dk=2\max_{k}d_{k}=2.
